newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Polish Solidarity vows support for market, growth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Polish Solidarity vows support for market, growth.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity trade union and the dozens of allied parties it is leading into this year's general election have drafted a programme that proclaims support for market principles and economic growth.
Solidarity chief Marian Krzaklewski, unveiling the draft this week, said it recognised that economic growth was vital for goals such as a better pension system, health care and education.
"A condition of achieving all those goals is the economic success of this programme, which will secure a high rate of growth," he said.
The programme has been welcomed by pro-market liberals associated with Solidarity Election Action (AWS), who are keen to ensure syndicalist or populist ideas do not take it over.

"This programme is a pleasant surprise...it is moderate and opens the way to many compromises..." said banker Andrzej Olechowski, a finance and foreign minister in past cabinets, commenting on advance leaks of the document.
"It stresses economic growth, lower taxes, decentralising the state and reforming public services," he said.
But analysts say the jury is still out on whether the AWS, which could win elections due in September, can put in place ministers suited to carrying out promises to speed reform.
AWS AIMS TO DISPEL DOUBTS ABOUT PRIORITIES

The 50 percent vote held by trade unionists in the AWS, which has sought state aid for the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard -- the birthplace of Solidarity under communism -- raises questions about the group's economic priorities.

Doubts also stem from statements by rightist parties in the group with populist ideas designed to appeal to Poland's many have-nots and a hunger to settle scores with ex-communists who have helped each other to prosper under the new system.
Such issues have been exploited by the ex-communists who portray themselves as the guardians of Western-style reform and the AWS as syndicalists arm-in-arm with extreme radicals.
AWS liberals said the programme dispelled these concerns.

"This programme has a clearly pro-market character...it is pro-NATO and pro-European, pro-market and focused on reforming the social services," said Czeslaw Bielecki, leader of the Ruch Stu (100 Movement) party on the pro-market wing of the AWS.

Bielecki told Reuters it was a sound compromise between the liberals' vision of an economy where private enterprise can flourish and the union's desire to heal public services and give more Poles a share of economic growth.
Such compromise was possible because both groups agreed they had to streamline government, overhaul the pension and health care system and ensure sustainable growth, he said.
The Catholic, traditionalist current in the AWS has also left its mark on the manifesto, which promotes a pro-family tax system, and promises to develop housing and educational reforms.
PROGRAMME SHUNS POLISH "THIRD WAY"

The programme shuns ideas voiced by some rightists of a Polish "third way between socialism and capitalism", calls for a one-off zloty devaluation to boost exports and economic vetting of the wealthy to ensure they are not corrupt ex-communists.
It makes a clear commitment to European Union entry, which some rightists embrace much less heartily than joining NATO.
The draft vows to seek a strong convertible zloty, and low inflation through capping public debt and deficits.

It returns to Solidarity's key idea of mass voucher-style privatisation but unlike some earlier proposals stresses supporting pension reform as its top goal and leaves room for strategic investors rather than a mere share-out of ownership.
But many analysts, including some insiders, say the AWS has yet to put on its list enough moderate, reform-minded candidates.

"If we have a predominance of Catholic and trade union activists the programme will be just window dressing...," said Olechowski, who was a Ruch Stu official but assumed a lower profile since the party joined the AWS.
"But if we have some kind of balance then...bingo! There will be nothing to worry about," he told Reuters.
Bielecki said the AWS had to embrace people with expertise, and be able to implement a reform package and lure centrist voters.
The AWS is now running neck-and-neck in opinion polls with the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of ex-communists turned social democrats, with up to 25 percent support each.

"If we fail to win over centrist voters and gain about 29-30 percent support...we will have many possible coalition options after the election but none of them will be capable of a decisive push with reforms," Bielecki said.
AWS liberals said the best option would be to form a government with the centrist Union for Freedom (UW) of Leszek Balcerowicz, who steered reform after communism fell in 1989.
"It's been a very difficult partner in the past but if we want to carry out reforms we need to have at least some kind of an agreement with them," said Bielecki.
DIFFICULT CHOICES AHEAD FOR AWS
But the AWS is torn between this option and tactical or ideological arguments for luring voters from further right.
The alliance campaigned mightily against a new constitution backed by both the ex-communists and the Union for Freedom.
Although it was narrowly defeated in the May 25 referendum, it gained backing for its stance with arguments that focused on rightist principles such as tightening abortion laws.
This separates it from the Union for Freedom, whose leader was scathing about the new Solidarity programme.
"This programme is inconsistent... just like the grouping which produced it," Balcerowicz said.

Some critics say that even though there is little chance the AWS or any other serious political force would depart from Poland's broad reform course, the alliance might yet lose its way amid ideological battles with the left.
Other commentators say that offering a smorgasboard of left-bashing, populism, pro-family talk and sensible economic thinking might be a highly effective campaign strategy.
"There is such a great demand for a grouping like this that voters will forgive it a lot of weaknesses," said Halina Franczak, analyst at the private Demoskop institute.
"The question is, how much discipline can its leaders show in the campaign to keep it within limits that would be acceptable for everyone," she said.
